rule: anchor -> next anchor of any skill, else session end

SYNTH-idle-gap.notes: index space is over UNIQUE API responses, after dedup: g0,g1,g2,g3

SYNTH-tag-hole.notes: A hole in the tag run. The rule splits it into two arcs, which is indistinguishable from a genuine re-invocation. Known and accepted -- the register treats re-invocation as a boundary anyway, so both readings agree on the boundary. Asserted here so the behaviour is pinned rather than merely documented: if Claude Code ever drops the tag mid-run, arcs fragment and per-routine cost shatters, and this test says so out loud.

SYNTH-long-run-then-anchor.notes: THE shape the rule exists for, and the only one in this fixture where a multi-turn anchor run is followed by another anchor. Run 0 is (start=0, tag_end=2), run 1 starts at 4, so the boundary must be next_run.start-1 = 3. Using next_run.tag_end (5) would claim turns 4 and 5 twice. Every other session's non-final runs have length 1, where start == tag_end and the two are indistinguishable -- real runs are median 15 turns, so this is the normal shape, not an edge case.

SYNTH-out-of-order.notes: File order is Oa(10:02), Oz(10:00), Om(10:01); timestamp order is Oz, Om, Oa. The ids are deliberately minted so their lexicographic order is the REVERSE of chronological order: sorting on message.id alone reverses the session, and sorting on file position alone puts the anchor at index 1. Only (timestamp, message.id) yields the anchor at index 0 and the arc [0..2]. Every other session's ids happen to sort in timestamp order, which would let the primary sort key be deleted unnoticed.

SYNTH-no-anchor.notes: No anchor anywhere. The whole session is unattributable. At full scale this is 6.0% of Opus notional list value ($1,416 across 48 sessions) -- the largest single component of the 7.4% remainder, so a rule that quietly dropped it would understate the labelled remainder most.

SYNTH-adjacent-anchors.notes: Two anchor runs directly adjacent, no untagged turn between. Every other multi-anchor session here has a gap, which lets a run-advance off-by-one skip the second anchor unnoticed; here it would drop a whole arc.

SYNTH-dup-and-tie.notes: Two traps at once. (1) The msg_synth_T2 group is written 2000, 500, 900 -- HIGH first. The SYNTH-idle-gap group is written low-then-high, where last-by-file-order happens to equal max; this one is its mirror, so the two together kill first-seen AND last-wins. Invariant 10 names both as wrong. (2) T0 (untagged) and T1 (anchored) share an identical timestamp, with T0 written first, so the (timestamp, message.id) tie-break decides the anchor's index. Sorting on timestamp alone leaves it order-dependent, which would make arc boundaries irreproducible (invariant 2b). The tied pair also breaks the 1:1 between message.id and requestId (T0 carries req_T9, T1 carries req_T1), so message.id and requestId order them oppositely: a tie-break on requestId would swap the anchor and the untagged turn. Real retries break that 1:1, which is why the dedup key is a pair and the sort key is not.

notes: Every dollar figure here is NOTIONAL LIST VALUE. Rates are the synthetic fixture's own registry, not production rates; they preserve the relative structure that matters (output 5x input, cache_write 1.25x, cache_read 0.1x) so mispricing cache_read as input fails a test.
